hints: Remember rate means change in concentration with time, so on a concentration against time curve you need the gradient at that instant, which means drawing a tangent at t = 40 s.
walkthrough:
See rate as steepness at one moment**
You are looking at how fast $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{CCl}$ is disappearing. On a concentration against time graph the rate at any instant is just how steep the curve is there. At t = 40 s the curve is sloping downwards, so draw a nice long tangent line that just touches the curve at 40 s.

Turn steepness into numbers**
Pick two widely spaced points on your tangent line, read off $\Delta y$ in $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ and $\Delta x$ in s, then calculate $\text{rate} = -\Delta[\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{CCl}]/\Delta t$. With a good tangent this gives about $$\text{rate} \approx 1.7 \times 10^{-4}\, \text{mol dm}^{-3}\text{s}^{-1}$$ Show the triangle and subtraction clearly.
Final answer: Draw tangent to curve at t = 40 s; rate = gradient = $1.70 \times 10^{-4}$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}\text{s}^{-1}$ (accept approx $1.6$ to $1.8 \times 10^{-4}$).

hints: Think what stays constant only for a first order curve and how you can read that from Fig. 3.1 using horizontal construction lines.
Plan to measure the time for concentration to fall to half its value at least twice, starting from different concentrations.
walkthrough:
Use the fingerprint of first order**
A first order decay has a very special habit. No matter where you start, it always takes the same time to halve. That constant half-life is your test. Zero and second order do not do this.

Read two halvings off the curve**
Start at $0.0200$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ at t = 0. Draw across to the curve at $0.0100$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ and down to time, about 30 s. Now start again at $0.0100$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ and go to $0.0050$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$, you get again about 30 s. You can also use $0.0140$ to $0.0070$ etc. Show the construction lines.

Link constant time to order**
Because the time to halve is essentially the same each time, $t_{1/2}$ is independent of concentration. That is only true for first order kinetics, so the overall reaction with methanol in large excess is first order.

Final answer: Measure successive half-lives from graph, e.g. $0.0200$ to $0.0100$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ takes ~30 s and $0.0100$ to $0.0050$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ takes ~30 s.
Half-life is constant, so reaction is first order in $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CCl}$ and hence overall first order.

hints: Convert 75% consumed into number of half-lives by thinking what fraction remains after one, then two halvings.
Recall the exact link between k and half-life for first order, $k = \ln 2 / t_{1/2}$, and what units k must have.
walkthrough:
Count the half-lives hidden in 75%**
After one half-life $50$% remains. After a second half-life half of that remains, so $25$% remains. That is exactly $75$% consumed. So 320 s must contain two half-lives. Therefore $$t_{1/2} = \frac{320}{2} = 160\,\text{s}$$

Convert half-life to k**
For first order only, $$k = \frac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}} = \frac{0.693}{160}$$ which gives $$k = 4.33 \times 10^{-3}\, \text{s}^{-1}$$ First order k always has units of $\text{s}^{-1}$ because rate ($\text{mol dm}^{-3}\text{s}^{-1}$) divided by concentration ($\text{mol dm}^{-3}$) leaves $\text{s}^{-1}$.

Final answer: $75$% consumed means $25$% remains = two half-lives, so $t_{1/2} = 320/2 = 160$ s.
$k = 0.693/160 = 4.33 \times 10^{-3}$ $\text{s}^{-1}$.

hints: Focus on what is being connected to what, and under what concentration, pressure and temperature conditions.
walkthrough:
Picture the comparison**
You can never measure one electrode on its own, you always compare it to the standard hydrogen electrode. Put your half-cell on one side, the SHE ($\text{Pt}$, $\text{H}_2$ at 1 atm, $\text{H}^+$ at 1 $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$, 298 K) on the other, join with wire and salt bridge, and read the voltmeter. That reading under all standard conditions is $E^{\ominus}$.
Final answer: The voltage / EMF measured when a half-cell is connected to a standard hydrogen electrode under standard conditions.

hints: Think what would happen to charge in each beaker if electrons leave one side and arrive at the other with no ions free to move.
walkthrough:
Keep each beaker neutral**
As electrons flow round the outer wire, one beaker becomes positive and the other negative. The salt bridge lets spectator ions drift across to cancel that build up, so current can keep flowing and the cell does not polarise. It completes the circuit while keeping the two solutions separate.
Final answer: Allows ions to move between half-cells to maintain charge balance / complete the circuit without mixing the electrolytes.

hints: Recall the two different types of half-cell here, a gas electrode on the left and a redox-in-solution electrode on the right, both needing inert Pt.
List what must be in each beaker, including $\text{H}_2$ gas supply for the SHE and both $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$, $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ together on the right.
Remember the numbers that make it standard, concentrations, gas pressure, temperature, plus the voltmeter in the external circuit.
walkthrough:
Build the hydrogen side**
On the left draw Pt foil dipping into $1$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ $\text{H}^+$(aq), with $\text{H}_2$ gas bubbled over it at 1 atm and 298 K. Pt is inert, it just carries electrons to the $2\text{H}^+ + 2\text{e}^- \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2$ equilibrium.

Build the dichromate side**
On the right there is no metal to use as electrode, so again use Pt. Dip it into a single solution containing $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$(aq), $\text{H}^+$(aq) and $\text{Cr}^{3+}$(aq), each at $1$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$. Label all three ions clearly.

Join and measure correctly**
Connect the two Pt electrodes with wires to a high resistance voltmeter so almost no current is drawn. Keep the given salt bridge between beakers. Add labels for 298 K and 1 atm $\text{H}_2$. That full labelling earns the marks.

Final answer: Left beaker (SHE): Pt electrode, $\text{H}_2$(g) with gas supply, $\text{H}^+$(aq) $1$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$, $298$ K, $1$ atm.
Right beaker: Pt electrode, $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$(aq) + $\text{H}^+$(aq) + $\text{Cr}^{3+}$(aq), all $1$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$.
High resistance voltmeter connecting the two Pt electrodes via wires; salt bridge joining solutions.

hints: Compare +1.33 V for dichromate with 0.00 V for SHE to decide which is more easily reduced and which sends electrons round the wire.
walkthrough:
Let the bigger $E^{\ominus}$ win**
$+1.33$ V is much more positive than $0.00$ V, so $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ is the stronger oxidising agent and gets reduced. The SHE is therefore oxidised, it is the negative pole. Electrons leave the SHE Pt and travel through the external circuit toward the dichromate Pt. Mark minus on the SHE and draw the arrow pointing away from it.
Final answer: SHE is the negative electrode; electrons flow in external wire away from SHE towards $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$/$\text{Cr}^{3+}$ electrode.

hints: Identify which Table 3.1 row is reduction ($\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$) and which must be reversed for oxidation (ethanal to ethanoic acid).
Balance electrons, 6e for dichromate against 2e for the organic couple, then subtract $E$ values as $E_{red} - E_{ox}$.
walkthrough:
Write the two halves the right way round**
Reduction is $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 14\text{H}^+ + 6\text{e}^- \rightleftharpoons 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Oxidation is the reverse of $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + 2\text{H}^+ + 2\text{e}^- \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{CHO} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$, so $\text{CH}_3\text{CHO} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + 2\text{H}^+ + 2\text{e}^-$.

Scale and add to cancel electrons**
Multiply the organic oxidation by 3 to give 6e to match dichromate. Adding and cancelling $6\text{e}^-$, $6\text{H}^+$ and $3\text{H}_2\text{O}$ leaves $$\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 3\text{CH}_3\text{CHO} + 8\text{H}^+ \rightleftharpoons 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 3\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

Calculate the cell voltage**
$$E_{cell}^{\ominus} = E_{red}^{\ominus} - E_{ox}^{\ominus} = (+1.33) - (-0.94) = +2.27\,\text{V}$$ The positive sign confirms feasibility under standard conditions.

Final answer: $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 3\text{CH}_3\text{CHO} + 8\text{H}^+ \rightleftharpoons 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 3\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$
$E_{cell}^{\ominus} = +1.33 - (-0.94) = +2.27$ V.

hints: Recall the link $\Delta G^{\ominus} = -nFE_{cell}^{\ominus}$ and find n from the $\text{O}_2 + 4\text{H}^+ + 4\text{e}^- \rightleftharpoons 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ half-equation.
Watch units, F is in $\text{C mol}^{-1}$ so the answer comes in J, then convert to $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ with correct sign.
walkthrough:
Pick out n, F and E**
The oxygen reduction moves 4 electrons, so $n = 4$. Use $F = 96500$ $\text{C mol}^{-1}$ and $E_{cell}^{\ominus} = +2.01$ V from the question. The governing relation is $$\Delta G^{\ominus} = -nFE_{cell}^{\ominus}$$ The minus sign tells you a positive cell voltage gives spontaneous negative free energy.

Substitute and convert**
$$\Delta G^{\ominus} = -4 \times 96500 \times 2.01 = -775860\,\text{J mol}^{-1}$$ Divide by 1000 for kJ: $$\Delta G^{\ominus} \approx -776\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$ Keep at least 3 significant figures and include the negative sign with units $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Final answer: $\Delta G^{\ominus} = -nFE_{cell}^{\ominus}$
$\Delta G^{\ominus} = -4 \times 96500 \times 2.01 = -775860$ $\text{J mol}^{-1} = -776$ $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ (3 s.f.).
